newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-Jittery S.African rand takes fresh dive.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Jittery S.African rand takes fresh dive.

text.p: For the second Tuesday in a row the South African rand plunged against the dollar, falling more than eight cents at one point to its weakest level since February 5.

Traders said the rand was hit by a repeat of cautious comments on the rand exchange rate from Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals, talk the central bank might quit the forward market and uncertainties about exchange control relaxation.
After a hectic afternoon session in which the currency swung from 4.42 against the dollar to a low of 4.4820, the rand finally steadied around 4.45 from 4.4135/4165 on Monday.
Dealers said the rot initially set in shortly before midday when dollar demand emerged after Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals reiterated comments made last week.

"The very sharp appreciation of the rand over the past six weeks was perhaps a little bit overdone. I don't really feel that the level of the exchange rate is overdone or that we should not have further appreciation, but I think one needs more gradual adjustments," Stals said.
Currency traders said the comments triggered dollar buying which pushed the rand from a morning's strongest level of 4.4080 bid to 4.42 by midday.
"Basically he believes that it may have been overdone on the downside and seems to be urging a bit of caution which is not an unhealthy thing," one trader said.
Rumours then surfaced that the Reserve Bank planned to withdraw from the forward rand market -- a move the central bank has said it plans to do without any shocks to the system.
Traders said the rumour appeared to be linked to a meeting between the central bank deputy governor James Cross and market players earlier in the day.
The central bank's forward foreign exchange position has risen to $20 billion, and a rapid unwinding could cause serious disruption in the foreign exchange market.
However, Cross told Reuters that discussions at the meeting were of a general and exploratory nature and the bank had no immediate plans to withdraw from the forward market.
"The only thing we might consider in time is maybe changing our pricing strategy, but that doesn't mean we can pull out of the market in the near term," he said.
Traders also pointed to Stals' comments that individuals were likely to benefit from moves on exchange controls, which raised anticipations of controls being removed sooner than expected.
Stals said earlier he would advise the government controls be relaxed to let individuals take money out of the country as part of the next phase of foreign exchange control relaxation.

Eric Beinstein, head of emerging markets at J.P. Morgan in London, told a Societe Generale Frankel Pollak investment conference that uncertainty about the impact of the removal of remaining foreign exchange controls was a major risk factor.
"That is the biggest fear of foreign investors," Beinstein said, adding it was unclear if inflows of capital would counter potential outflows as residents were feared to invest overseas.
Concerns about the lifting of exchange controls played a pivotal role in the near 30 percent depreciation of the rand against the dollar in 1996.

Beinstein said the rand was currently trading at a discount of around 11 percent to its five-year moving average following its fall last year. But examples from other countries suggested that deviation from the five-year trend line could be a long-term phenomenon.
